lessons.title: Three ways a call can enter
objectives: Refuse to treat a Cisco gateway as a UCCX import
paragraphs: The technical requirements describe three SIP stories. Five9 can provide ITSP trunks. Your ITSP can connect to Five9 session border controllers, and there is a checklist for that. Or a gateway you already own — Avaya, Cisco, or Asterisk — can talk to Five9 over the internet, a VPN, or Direct Connect.
Cisco in that sentence is a gateway type, not a promise that a UCCX script will import. Pick the story before you draw a codec or a DNIS.

lessons.title: DNS, codecs, and the default voice
objectives: Keep G.711 as the default you can cite
paragraphs: The requirements prefer DNS SRV for the SIP targets. G.711 is the default codec, and the PDF describes it as uncompressed. Do not invent a packetization time. A 20 millisecond ptime shows up in practitioner notes about Cisco gateways. It is not a number this lab will attribute to the Five9 PDF.
RFC 3261 is the SIP signaling baseline. RFC 4733 is the telephone-event way digits often ride once the call is up. DTMF design is a separate sentence from the codec.

lessons.title: How much bandwidth a seat costs
paragraphs: The requirements give planning numbers. Agent Desktop Plus and the Plus adapters are 128 kbps. The Java agent is 88 kbps. Agent Assist adds about 12 kbps. A VPN adds about 64. CRM or other business apps add about 64. A UC client such as Teams, Zoom, Office@Hand, RingCentral, or Nextiva is called out around 320 kbps.

One-way latency should stay under 150 ms. Wi-Fi is acceptable when the bandwidth is actually there. Wired is preferred. Satellite is not supported. Cellular and 5G are not supported. Those are support statements, not opinions.

lessons.title: NAT, idle timers, and split tunnels
paragraphs: NAT and PAT are acceptable. Double NAT is not. UDP bindings that idle out cause one-way audio. The requirements use a 30 second UDP idle timeout as the planning number, and they tell you to send keepalives when the binding is shorter.

On a VPN, translate RFC 1918 space to a public address the far side can route. Do not exclude Five9 domains from a split tunnel and then wonder why signaling dies. Do not restrict SIP or RTP between sites.

lessons.title: Direct Connect and the edges
paragraphs: Direct Connect in the requirements is a Layer-3 handoff. There is no Layer-2 requirement. The port is 10, 100, or 1000 full duplex, and failover uses BGP. Equinix Fabric edges named in the PDF this lab read are Chicago CH3, Washington DC10, London LD5, Amsterdam AM4, Frankfurt FR8, São Paulo SP4, Tokyo TY11, and Sydney SY5.
Those city codes are a snapshot. A new PDF can add or retire an edge. Write the date next to the list before a circuit is ordered.

lessons.title: TLS, and ports that are not universal
objectives: Keep Studio ports in the Studio box
paragraphs: Unencrypted APIs are not the story. TLS 1.2 is required. TLS 1.1 is not supported. The requirements also list TLS 1.3 inbound ciphers: AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, and CHACHA20.

Studio portal hosts and Studio SIP ports live in the Studio section of that PDF: UDP 5060, TCP 5061 described as beta, proxy UDP 5189 and TCP 5161, a legacy UDP 5188, plus RTP ranges. Do not paste those Studio numbers onto every VCC ITSP trunk. If the trunk guide does not say them, they are not the trunk.

lessons.title: Headsets, and the call that only fails one way
objectives: Check Efficiency Mode before you blame the trunk
paragraphs: USB noise-canceling headsets are the recommendation. Analog headsets are not supported. Wireless is not recommended once you are above roughly ten agents. Windows 11 Efficiency Mode can drop live calls. Java admin is not the Mac ARM path; use the web admin there. None of that is a SIP trunk, and all of it still stops a call.

When audio fails, walk the stack this track just built: path type, codec, bandwidth medium, NAT, TLS, then the headset. The topology tool lets you pull the ITSP or the SBC and hear the symptom described. It is a model.
